item.title: Intermolecular and Interfacial Origins of Layering in a Near-Isotropic Organic Glass Former
item.description: arXiv:2611.00223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical vapor deposition can produce organic glasses with enhanced stability and pronounced structural anisotropy (layering) even when the constituent molecules are nearly spherical. However, the microscopic origin of the layering in spherical molecular glass formers remains unclear. We investigated vapor-deposited films of 9-(3,5-di(naphthalen-1-yl)phenyl)anthracene ({\alpha},{\alpha}-A) by grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering, atomistic molecular dynamics, and coarse-grained simulations. Experimentally, the layering signal varies nonmonotonically with deposition temperature and is strongest near 0.8T_g. Simulated scattering calculations reproduce the principal experimental features and show that the layering peak does not originate from shifts in single molecule degrees of freedom. In fact, the simulated deposited and bulk glasses show largely the same single-molecule conformations. Interestingly, a one-site coarse-grained liquid with isotropic interactions develops a comparable interfacial layering signature. These results indicate that layering in {\alpha},{\alpha}-A arises primarily from collective density correlations generated at the free surface during deposition rather than from conformational bias or orientational ordering. The findings connect structural anisotropy in vapor-deposited molecular glasses to the generic interfacial organization of simple liquids.
item.dc:creator: Charles H. Carroll, Juliana I. Bonilla-Lugo, Arthur Y. Lin, Richard Stephens, Peng Luo, Sarah E. Wolf, Cindy Yueli Chen, Dong Hyup Kim, Yu Wu, Patrick J. Walsh, Patryk W\k{a}sik, Whitney S. Loo, Zahra Fahkraai, Rose K. Cersonsky

item.title: Impact of Surface Preparation on the Propulsion of Catalytic Janus Colloids and Implications for Reproducibility
item.description: arXiv:2611.00274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) Janus particles (JPs) propelled by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are a widely used model system for active matter, yet reported speeds for similar particles and fuel concentrations differ by more than an order of magnitude. Broad adoption of these materials requires increasing consistency in the preparation and achieving improved repeatability in their behavior. Herein, we focused on two routine, but rarely reported, preparation steps that we found to alter the particle speed. First, we found that pre-exposing the platinum cap to H2O2 before cell assembly increased the mean speed by a factor of 2.4. The size of this effect depended on batch history, where an aged batch responded strongly, while a freshly prepared batch sped up by only 16%. Second, we found that plasma cleaning of the glass substrate decreased the speed 2.7 times. In a 120 $\mu$m cell the suppression was the same at both walls even when only one wall was treated. The suppression grew with the treated glass area per unit fluid volume, which pointed to species released into the bulk solution rather than to a change at the wall. Plasma-cleaned glass released more ions into water than untreated glass, and XPS detected an ionic metal fluoride on the plasma-cleaned surface. A model in which the released ions lower the speed through the solution conductivity reproduced the measured speeds in all four cell geometries. Of the 17 published studies compared here, pre-activation is reported in only four studies and substrate cleaning in only six studies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for the preparation and associated speed measurements of catalytic Janus particles.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Haroon (Case Western Reserve University), Mitchell Lau (Case Western Reserve University), Christopher L. Wirth (Case Western Reserve University)

item.title: Multistable elastic pixels: nematic elasticity for non-volatile positioning of colloidal optical scatterers
item.description: arXiv:2611.00318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-volatile reconfiguration of optical devices, in which a configuration persists without continuous energy input, remains a challenge. We introduce multistable elastic pixels (MEPs), lithographically defined pores filled with a nematic liquid crystal, whose curved ends capture a scattering inclusion in one of two mechanically stable sites. Simulations and experiments show that pore geometry and homeotropic surface anchoring define the energy minima and the height of the barrier between them. This barrier far exceeds thermal energies, stabilizing a scatterer location absent an external field. Colloidal inclusions switch reversibly between sites under transient electric fields. Using arrays of static scatterers, we show that the two positional states produce distinct responses at visible wavelengths, demonstrating the potential of MEPs for reconfigurable devices and metasurfaces. Unlike phase-change and liquid-crystal-tuned approaches, which switch a material surrounding fixed scatterers, MEPs use the nematoelastic energy landscape to move the optical element itself.
item.dc:creator: Jed-Joan S. Edziah, Brian Edwards, Nader Engheta, Kathleen J. Stebe

item.title: Kinetics of pollutant adsorption onto polymers: the Langevin dynamics study
item.description: arXiv:2611.00358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study adsorption kinetics of low-molecular-weight adsorbate particles on a polymer via the Langevin dynamics. The impact of the polymer molecular weight and of the strength of the polymer-particle attraction are examined. We consider mixtures of $n_p$ chains of the length $N$ with adsorbate, where $n_pN=600$ holds. Analysis includes examination of visualizations and evaluation of adsorption capacity, binding energy, average gyration radius, and asphericity of the polymer-adsorbate complexes. Both adsorption capacity and total binding energy show monotonic, logistic-like behavior; the former reaches a plateau sooner than the latter does, indicating further optimization of the maximum-capacity complex. Binding energy per particle and asphericity of complexes both demonstrate non-trivial behaviors, with distinct extrema at the intermediate stages of adsorption. The analysis reveals three stages of adsorption: (i) formation of small polymer-particle complexes, (ii) gradual merge of these into a single complex, (iii) stationary state. The stage (i) completes faster for short chains, as in this case fewer conformational rearrangements are required. The stage (ii) completes faster for long chains because of the necklace-like arrangement of small complexes along a long chain, which promotes their merge vs. diffusion-driven merge of the complexes of short chains. Our results indicate that for the rapid removal of pollutants in the high interaction regime, it is more effective to use the set of short polymer chains. On the other hand, long linear chains are optimal for adsorbing pollutants in a weak interaction regime.
item.dc:creator: K. Haydukivska, V. Blavatska, Ja. Ilnytskyi

item.title: Non-Equilibrium Statistical Mechanics of Glass-Forming Liquids under Continuous Cooling: Microscopic Inner Clocks, Fictive Temperatures, and Kauzmann Diagrams
item.description: arXiv:2611.00382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The description of macroscopic properties in out-of-equilibrium amorphous solids such as gels and glasses, typically processed under finite cooling rates, remains a fundamental challenge for modern statistical physics. In this work, we employ the Non-Equilibrium Self-Consistent Generalized Langevin Equation (NESCGLE) theory to construct a microscopic description of the structural and calorimetric glass transition under continuous cooling. Building upon the microscopic Onsager-Machlup interpretation of Narayanaswamy's material time (the inner clock $u(t)$) [J.Chem.Phys. 156, 244506 (2022)], we recover Tool's fictive temperature $T_f$ directly from the evolving spatial pair correlations and show that wavenumber dispersion naturally generalizes the classical scalar $T_f$ into a continuous mode spectrum governed by de Gennes narrowing at the primary cage peak. Across wide variations in cooling rate down to the quasi-static limit, the theory yields first-principles non-equilibrium Kauzmann diagrams for the two-body excess entropy that dynamically avert the Kauzmann crisis above the ideal dynamic arrest temperature $T_c$, while predicting sigmoidal relaxational heat-capacity steps consistent with computer simulations and calorimetry. Finally, we extract the cooling-rate-dependent glass transition temperature $T_g(q)$ from both equal-area integrals and differential heat-capacity landmarks, demonstrating that its asymptotic approach toward $T_c$ obeys a critical power-law scaling governed directly by the equilibrium dynamic arrest exponent.
item.dc:creator: R. Peredo-Ortiz, M. Medina-Noyola, L. F. Elizondo-Aguilera

item.title: Colloidal gel morphology and phase behavior differs based on the electrostatic interaction model in concentrated electrolytes
item.description: arXiv:2611.00419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting how nanoparticles interact in concentrated electrolytes remains a central challenge in nanoscience, with implications spanning energy storage, catalysis, and soft materials design. While Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) theory provides a widely used framework for modeling colloidal interactions, its electrostatic component relies on electric double-layer (EDL) theories whose validity in ionic liquids and concentrated electrolytes is consistently debated. Experiments have revealed significant deviations from classical screening behavior, including underscreening and oscillatory charge ordering, yet the consequences of these nonclassical effects for collective nanoparticle behavior remain unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that the extended range and oscillatory nature of electrostatic screening in concentrated electrolytes predicts different phase behavior and morphology of colloidal ionogels, yielding distinct thermodynamic signatures, percolation thresholds, and amorphous network structures. Using molecular dynamics simulations with DLVO-type pair interactions parameterized by competing EDL models, we systematically compare the consequences of different screening theories on gel formation and configurations.
item.dc:creator: Hwigwang Lim, Caleb Youngwerth, Lisa Je, Matthew Gebbie, Rose K. Cersonsky

item.title: Measuring structural restraint in an amorphous material using the variance of speckle intensity
item.description: arXiv:2611.00583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An experimentally accessible measure of structural restraint in supercooled liquids is defined based on the variance of the intensity of speckle pattern arising from elastic scattering of coherent radiation. Using simulation data, the resulting measure of structural restraint is shown to correlate with the temperature dependence of the shear modulus and the Debye-Waller factor. The paper includes consideration of the influence of the choice of the scattering wavevector and the degree of coarse graining used in intensity measurements on the measured restraint.
item.dc:creator: Charlotte F. Petersen, Peter Harrowell

item.title: Kinetics of Self-Organization in One Component Active Matter Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.00618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an inherently nonequilibrium system consisting of self-propelled particles using molecular dynamics simulation in $d=2$. The system self-organizes through quorum-sensing interactions characterized by an interaction range $\lambda$ and a parameter $c_{\mathrm{th}}$. When the local concentration sensed by a particle, represented by an auxiliary variable $c_i(t)$ exceeds $c_{\mathrm{th}}$, its self-propulsion velocity abruptly drops to zero, leading to the emergence of particle rich domains. For small $\lambda$, we observe a droplet-like morphology of clusters, which crosses over to a bicontinuous structure as $\lambda$ increases. We confirm this transition by computing the eccentricity of the domains. Next, we characterize the evolving domain morphologies using equal-time correlation function $C(r,t)$ and structure factor $S(k,t)$ of the density field. For a fixed $\lambda$, the scaled $C(r,t)$'s at different times are indistinguishable from each other, indicating dynamical scaling. However, at a fixed time $t$, the scaling functions differ for different values of $\lambda$, confirming a $\lambda$-dependent morphological transition. In the large-wavevector limit ($k\rightarrow\infty$), the tail of $S(k,t)$ consistently follows the Porod's law: $S(k,t)\sim k^{-3}$. Furthermore, the average domain size $L(t)$ exhibits a power-law growth, $L(t)\sim t^{1/3}$, independent of $\lambda$.
item.dc:creator: Avinash Chauhan, Prasenjit Das

item.title: Rapid microscopic decorrelation precedes sustained collective ordering in quenched two-dimensional colloids
item.description: arXiv:2611.01192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Independent Brownian noise can rapidly separate trajectories launched from the same microscopic configuration, but configuration-space distance need not reveal their later assembly outcomes. We studied this distinction in 480 two-dimensional Brownian-dynamics trajectories generated as three independent-noise replicas of 40 parent configurations under four finite-duration quenches. Ninety-two of 160 replica sets sharing one parent and one protocol reached both ordered and non-ordered terminal outcomes. A relative-diffusion calculation relates the free-particle mean-squared replica separation to the time-integrated diffusivity. The measured mean-squared separation remained about one-sixth of the free-particle reference, while its scaling was indistinguishable for replica pairs with the same and different outcomes. In contrast, outcome-resolved global sixfold order, ordered-particle population and coherence, and reciprocal-space translational order separated progressively after quench completion. With quench durations weighted equally, global order, the state score combining global and population order, coherence, and translational order remained informative 0.50 reduced time units before terminal assessment. This result persisted after either changing the terminal window or reducing the integration timestep. Transient threshold crossings were common, and 94.5\% of non-ordered crossings subsequently lost the required ordered-particle population. An independent $N=128$ ensemble showed state-score discrimination at temperatures for which both terminal classes occurred. The assembly dynamics therefore separate generic microscopic decorrelation from the later emergence and finite-window persistence of collective order associated with terminal structure.
item.dc:creator: Ruixin Zhou, Boliang Yu

item.title: Compliance-Shifting Elastogranular Shells
item.description: arXiv:2611.01278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shells and grains separately exhibit complex nonlinear behavior when confined - shells buckle and snap, while grains transition from fluid-like to solid-like. When coupled, elastogranular structures have the ability to display a remarkable variety of mechanical behaviors. Gere we created an elastogranular shell where spherical grains are sandwiched between two thin, elastic shells. By evacuating the air enclosed by the two layers, we can tune the stiffness of the elastogranular shell and alter its critical buckling load. Introducing controlled vacancy defects in the arrangement of the grains allows us to more finely tune critical buckling parameters, as the shell must balance the combined effects of defect size and resultant granular packing density. Defects in the jammed granular layer have a counterintuitive effect on the shell's buckling load, as they can stiffen the shell away from the defect. With an empirically determined scaling model, we established how the shell and grains distribute load and create a compliance-shifting structure with a tunable buckling load.
item.dc:creator: Jairaj Narendran, Paolo Limcaoco, Shashank S. Basty, Douglas P. Holmes

item.title: Valence-Selective Electrophoretic Transport in Neutral Carbon Nanotubes
item.description: arXiv:2611.02077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how confinement alters the transport of charged molecules is central to the advancement of separation, energy, and sensing technologies. Polyamines are small, linear molecules with ionizable groups, making them an ideal model for investigating charge transport in confinement beyond monatomic ions. Using all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we investigate how molecular length, net charge, and charge placement affect the electrophoretic transport of polyamines through single-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs). We find that nanometer-scale confinement reverses the mobility ordering observed in free solution -- in a CNT of radius 0.68 nm, spermine (q = +4) travels more slowly than ethylamine (q = +1), contrasting with the expected scaling of mobility with valence in bulk. Further, we find that mobility decreases faster than the inverse of valence, though molecular size and length vary alongside this trend. Comparisons of doubly protonated spermidine microspecies reveal the additional influence of charge placement at fixed net valence. Upon moving one proton of dicationic spermidine from the central to a terminal nitrogen, the mobility is increased by 42%. We analyze hydration structure and solute-solvent association, identifying local-solvation differences between protonation topologies that accompany these distinct transport responses under confinement. These results suggest that neutral CNTs could support valence-selective nanofluidic transport, with additional sensitivity to molecular structure and protonation topology.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Mattia Amato, Felipe Jim\'enez-\'Angeles, Monica Olvera de la Cruz

item.title: Phase behavior of a two-dimensional suspension of active pentagons
item.description: arXiv:2611.02176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Applying insights acquired when studying idealized particle systems to real-world amorphous materials remains a significant challenge, primarily due to the complex interplay between particles' shape and interaction mechanisms. It is known that regular pentagons do not tessellate the two dimensional plane, making them the simplest regular polygons unable to form periodic tiling. This geometric constraint, combined with the complexity of interactions among non-spherical particles, may give rise to rich emergent behaviors, especially when dealing with self-propelled pentagons. Thus, geometry, interactions, and self-propulsion collectively lead to novel dynamical emerging phases. In this context, we investigate how activity and excluded-volume interactions affect the collective behavior of a two-dimensional suspension of active pentagon-shaped particles. Our results reveal that active pentagons not only undergo an arrested motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) but, under given conditions, they form traveling/rotating clusters exhibiting translational/chiral motion. Interestingly, both phases present an enhanced stability due to particles' activity, shape and excluded-volume interactions, forming an ice-ray lattice whose internal structure represents the densest packing fraction a two-dimensional pentagon suspension may achieve.
item.dc:creator: R. Fern\'andez-Quevedo Garc\'ia, B. Wu-Zhang, C. M. Barriuso G., W. Lin, M. Ruiz-Garc\'ia, H. Xiao, C. Valeriani

item.title: Modeling Crystallization in Concentrated Suspensions of Compressible Microgels
item.description: arXiv:2611.02184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Soft colloidal particles, such as microgels, made of cross-linked polymer gels that can swell by absorbing a good solvent, have internal degrees of freedom that allow them to respond to external stimuli by changing size. Sensitive responses to variations in temperature and concentration have inspired many practical applications, e.g., to drug delivery, biosensing, filtration, and photonic crystals. At sufficiently high concentrations, mutual crowding can drive microgels to interpenetrate or deform by faceting. To explore the influence of particle softness and compressibility on thermodynamic phase stability, we develop a coarse-grained model in which spherical microgels interact via the Hertz elastic pair potential and can respond to crowding by deswelling and faceting or interpenetrating, as governed by the Flory-Rehner theory of polymer networks. In our model, faceting reduces the volume available for swelling, while interpenetration affects polymer solvent mixing entropy. By performing Monte Carlo simulations that incorporate novel trial changes in particle size and shape, we compute equilibrium swelling ratios and Lindemann ratios to determine the fluid-solid phase stability boundary over a range of particle softness, tuned by varying cross-link fraction. Predictions from our facet model are in qualitative agreement with experiments and molecular-scale simulations. In contrast to the phase behavior of incompressible Hertzian spheres, we find that suspensions of compressible microgels crystallize at significantly lower volume fractions when accounting for the free energy costs of faceting and interpenetration. Our results extend previous studies of microgel phase behavior and can help to interpret experiments.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: O. E. Alade and A. R. Denton, Soft Matter 22, 5463 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Oreoluwa E. Alade, Alan R. Denton

item.title: The maximum packing fraction of disordered bidisperse discs: theory and predictions
item.description: arXiv:2611.02805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting the highest packing fraction that disordered packing of bidisperse discs can achieve, $\phi_{max}$, is an important unresolved problem. Such a predictive theory is hindered by the density dependence on the packing protocol and by ensuring disorder. In bidisperse packings, this is more complicated because $\phi_{max}$ is not a number but a function of the disc species size ratio, $D$, and one of the disc species concentration, $p$. These difficulties have been overcome in monodisperse disc packings by using the cell order distribution (COD)~\cite{Bl21}. Focusing on size ratios that prohibit rattlers, a COD-based theory is constructed here. It introduces bidisperse statistical closure equations, which combine an explicit disorder criterion with consistent cell and edge statistics, and yields $\phi_{max}(p,D)$ and structural predictions. The a-priori disorder-guaranteeing criterion proposed here ensures fast exponential a decay of the occurrence probability of ordered clusters with size. Using a constrained maximum-entropy analysis to ensure maximum disorder, the occurrence probabilities of all the possible cell and edge configurations are derived in terms of $p$ and $D$ and they are found to be binomial. All the results are assembled to yield an exact prediction of $\phi_{max}(p,D)$.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Blumenfeld

item.title: Membrane particle wrapping across methods and shapes
item.description: arXiv:2611.03310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the passive wrapping of adhesive particles by lipid membranes is a crucial step in untangling more complex endocytotic processes. However, despite the variety of computational approaches used to study passive endocytosis, a direct comparison of results across different modeling methods has never been performed. In this work, we present a comparative analysis of three distinct frameworks: numerical solutions of the axisymmetric membrane shape equation, a particle-based molecular dynamics model (MesoMem), and an energy-based triangulated surface model (FreeDTS). First, we validated our numerical solver for spherical particles against established literature and extended the implementation to include closed vesicle membranes and non-spherical particles. Next, we studied the same system with our two simulation methods, and found that the phase plots obtained from our numerical solution agree with those from our simulations. We then extended our study to anisotropic particles. By tracking engulfment pathways in MesoMem and FreeDTS, we observed a dynamic rotational transition where non-spherical particles initially bind in a horizontal ('submarine') orientation and subsequently rotate to a vertical ('rocket') orientation to complete wrapping - a behavior impossible to capture with standard axisymmetric models. Lastly, we considered the wrapping of soft vesicles with FreeDTS. Our simulations of a deformable, fixed-connectivity particle show that stronger adhesion promotes wrapping, whereas increasing membrane tension suppresses it. Complete engulfment is accompanied by a substantial reduction in particle volume, suggesting that particle compressibility provides an additional pathway for wrapping.
item.dc:creator: Pietro Sillano, Haochun Sun, B. Yolda\c{s} Cinemre, Timon Idema

item.title: Polarity-Programmed Topological Gating of Knotting in Spatially Patterned Active Polymers
item.description: arXiv:2611.03474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatially patterned tangential activity provides a route to program polymer topology through both geometry and propulsion direction. We use Langevin-dynamics simulations of a flexible, self-avoiding linear polymer to determine how active-domain placement and independently assigned propulsion polarities control nonequilibrium knotting. Reversing the polarities of two terminal active blocks switches the steady state from a nearly always-knotted regime to effective knot suppression, changing the knotting probability by more than three orders of magnitude despite identical active-block positions and activity magnitude. Across symmetric terminal two-block architectures, we further identify an approximate zero-one-two free-end-alignment rule: zero, one, and two free-end-aligned active blocks correspond, respectively, to suppressed, intermediate, and high-knotting states. A two-state kinetic decomposition shows that the conditional knot-formation rate changes only by about threefold under polarity reversal, whereas the mean knot lifetime changes by several orders of magnitude, demonstrating that knot survival and passive-region storage dominate the polarity-controlled switch. Block placement provides an additional geometrical gate: moving an active domain from the chain interior to a terminal region strongly enhances both knot formation and survival. Knot-center residence, knotted-arc distributions, and episode-resolved kymographs reveal formation near free-end-aligned active blocks, directed contour migration, tightening, and long-lived retention in passive regions. Together, these results support a source-conveyor-reservoir-sink mechanism in which signed polarity and spatial activity patterning control whether knots are generated, transported, stored, or rapidly lost, providing a route to programmable topological states in nonequilibrium active polymers.
item.dc:creator: Shiqi Zhou

item.title: Modeling and Analysis of Cooling Induced Isotropic Nematic Transitions in Pharmaceutical Liquid Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2611.00273v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper studies the phase transition from an isotropic to a nematic liquid crystal driven by controlled cooling, motivated by the manufacturing of next-generation pharmaceutical drugs. Using the non-isothermal Ericksen model for liquid crystals with a variable degree of orientation, we formulate the problem as a stiff, quasilinear system of parabolic partial differential equations. We establish a consistent thermodynamic framework, prove the well-posedness of the system, and conduct a rigorous asymptotic and numerical scaling analysis of the moving phase boundary in a cylindrical cell subjected to bottom-wall convective cooling. Our analysis identifies a critical sample thickness that separates two distinct physical regimes. Below this threshold, the transition follows the cooling dynamics and the material remains quasi-isothermal. Above the thickness threshold, bulk thermal diffusion governs the dynamics, imposing a dominant thermal delay characterized by a concave quadratic propagation front. These results demonstrate that scaling from laboratory characterization to industrial production fundamentally alters the spatial thermal history of the material, providing a predictive mathematical framework to optimize cooling protocols for kinetic arrest.
item.dc:creator: Pei Liu, Debanjan Banerjee, Daniel Siebel-Cortopassi, Sichen Song, Maria-Carme Calderer

item.title: Ewald summation of doubly periodic 2- and 3-dimensional Stokes multipoles
item.description: arXiv:2611.00308v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In spite of the qualitative differences between Stokes flows in 2 and 3 dimensions, most particle-resolved computational studies of microswimmers and other colloidal systems dominated by low-Re hydrodynamic interactions are carried out in triply periodic geometries, while the corresponding continuum descriptions are frequently solved in 2-dimensional doubly periodic domains. Furthermore, most experimental examples of biological and synthetic microswimmers are realised in confined, quasi-2-dimensional geometries with a finite thickness in one of the three dimensions. To enable studying the non-trivial differences between these system geometries, in this paper we systematically derive Ewald representations for periodic Stokes force multipoles in geometries with two periodic directions, treating both three-dimensional Stokes flow with one unbounded coordinate and intrinsically two-dimensional singularities. Starting from the periodic Stokeslet, we obtain explicit expressions for force dipoles and quadrupoles and analyse the non-trivial zero-wavevector contribution arising under partial periodicity. The analytical expressions are independently validated by comparing with results from an explicit lattice Boltzmann solver in each geometry.
item.dc:creator: Teunike A. van de Pol, Zhan Ma, Alexander Morozov, Joakim Stenhammar

item.title: Beyond Synthesis Conditions: Linking In-situ Growth Dynamics to Carbon Nanotube Forest Properties through Multimodal Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.00739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning for chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has largely mapped static synthesis conditions to final properties, implicitly treating these conditions as a complete description of growth. Here, we test this assumption by integrating gas-flow conditions with in-situ time-resolve growth profiles (growth curves) of vertically aligned CNT forests. We introduce an observation-window analysis, in which prediction is evaluated as a function of observation time by providing models with the growth curve only up to progressively later times, to determine not only whether a property can be predicted, but when the necessary information becomes available during synthesis. Clustering of normalized growth curves revealed distinct growth patterns independent of final forest height. The gas conditions alone could predict the initial growth rate but not the growth lifetime and failed to capture the variation in yield (R^2<0). Adding the growth curve improved yield prediction (R^2~0.4-0.5), with the relevant information emerging during the intermediate and later stages of growth rather than at its onset. In contrast, density and G/D ratio, which forest height does not record, showed no consistent improvement. The maximum height and lifetime could be estimated with moderate accuracy midway through the 10-min growth. Permutation feature importance identified water vapor and H_2, both linked to catalyst activity, as the most informative gas variables. These results indicate that variation unexplained by synthesis conditions is not merely noise but reflects an evolving catalyst state, and they establish mid-growth decision points for autonomous synthesis, enabling early termination of unpromising batches and, ultimately, in-batch adjustment of growth conditions.
item.dc:creator: Shun Muroga, Takashi Tsuji, Shunsuke Sakurai, Don N Futaba

item.title: Canonic hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium: Reassessing the role of cooperativity
item.description: arXiv:2611.00824v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium is normally studied within the grand canonical ensemble, which assumes that each hemoglobin is immersed in a reservoir of unbound oxygen molecules of the plasma. We show that this assumption is incorrect inside the RBC (red blood cell or erythrocyte), where the hemoglobin concentration is larger than the concentration of unbound oxygen in plasma. We suggest a better model, where a single hemoglobin and a few oxygen molecules around it reach a canonical equilibrium at a fixed volume (determined from the RBC structure) and a fixed temperature. The basic models of hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium -- Pauling's model and Monod-Wyman-Changeux model -- can be reformulated for this canonical situation. They predict cooperative interaction energies, which are significantly lower than predictions of the same models in the grand canonical ensemble. Larger cooperative energies, in particular those predicted by the grand canonical ensemble, lead to instabilities (cascade processes) in oxygen release within the canonical approach. Oxygen-binding fluctuations within this approach are sizably smaller than those in the grand canonical situation. These results suggest that the hopping diffusion of oxygen from one hemoglobin to another may play a role in oxygen diffusion within the RBC.
item.dc:creator: A. E. Allahverdyan, S. G. Gevorkian, A. Harutyunyan, Y. Sh. Mamasakhlisov, V. Stepanyan

item.title: Extended Onsager's variational principle for nonlinear chemical reaction kinetics in active matter
item.description: arXiv:2611.01131v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Onsager's variational principle (OVP) constructs dissipative dynamics from free energy, dissipation, and input power, but deterministic rate laws alone do not identify fluctuations or chemical fuel consumption. We examine these distinctions for nonlinear reaction kinetics in active matter. Comparing Gaussian diffusion and Poisson reaction events clarifies when statistical fluctuations match a physical Rayleighian: the reaction dissipation potential must be consistent with counting statistics, local detailed balance links rate bias to chemical affinity, and kinetic scales remain constitutive inputs. Under these conditions, the normalized Rayleighian excess gives the leading rate-fluctuation cost in the frozen-state, many-event regime. Three models illustrate the consequences. Spatially uniform reactions exhibit protocol-dependent nonreciprocal response compatible with fixed-state OVP; different Rayleighian representations can select the same rate without specifying the same fluctuations. In an active emulsion, a finite fuel pool accounts for free-energy transfer and dissolution of a chemically maintained domain after replenishment stops. In a membrane-cytosol model, distinct reaction-channel realizations yield identical protein-density trajectories but different chemical input power. Under a separate kinetic assumption, an exact total-density equation still requires an initial rate and does not determine chemical work or fluctuations. These results clarify the physical and statistical inputs required for constructing reaction-transport models and interpreting their fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: Xinpeng Xu, Changhao Li, Zhongqiang Xiong, Bin Zheng, Kento Yasuda, Shigeyuki Komura

item.title: From First Bond to Stable Adhesion: Multivalent Bond Stabilization in Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.01293v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: After a particle forms its first receptor--ligand bond near a cell membrane, stable attachment often requires a threshold number of additional bonds. This paper develops a biophysical kinetic theory of this post-capture stage. The bond-number dynamics are modeled as a finite birth--death chain on $n=0,1,\dots,m$, where $0$ is loss of the initial bond and $m$ is the stabilization threshold. The mesoscopic rates $\lambda_n$ and $\mu_n$ encode the local energy landscape, accessible receptor--ligand pairs, steric and orientational constraints, and cooperative interactions within the growing cluster. The probability of reaching the threshold before losing the first bond is derived in closed form for general rates and, in the constant-ratio case, reduces to a geometric series controlled by the free-energy bias $\rho_n=\mu_n/\lambda_n$. The mean time to failure or stabilization follows from a tridiagonal backward equation. Conditioning on successful attachment is treated as a trajectory-selection effect: the conditioned chain is a Doob $h$-transform whose dissociation rate at $n=1$ vanishes, because successful trajectories cannot lose the first bond early. A minimal interface between the spatial first-capture probability and the bond-number chain is formulated, together with the conditions under which the stable capture probability factorizes into their product. The analysis shows that hitting probabilities constrain only the rate ratios, whereas the absolute rate scale requires time-resolved or dwell-time data. The threshold $m$ is a model-defined stabilization criterion, not a directly measured ligand count. The rates and threshold are effective parameters specified independently or inferred from kinetic data. The theory provides a quantitative framework for interpreting attachment probabilities, lifetimes, and the transition from first bond formation to stable multivalent adhesion.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu

item.title: Before the First Bond: Depletion-Assisted Stochastic Capture at the Onset of Endocytosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.01321v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In a crowded extracellular environment, viruses and nanoparticles must reach the cell membrane within a few nanometers before the first ligand-receptor bond can form. Crowders generate an entropic depletion attraction, yet continuum models usually assume contact is already established or treat the approach deterministically. We formulate a thermodynamically consistent stochastic theory for this pre-contact stage. The sphere-plane depletion geometry uses the exact Asakur-Oosawa spherical-cap overlap, rather than a fitted cap, with either ideal van 't Hoff or pressure-only Carnahan-Starling osmotic pressure. A spatially varying near-wall mobility introduces a noise-induced drift that is essential for thermodynamic consistency and is often omitted. The first specific reaction is modeled by a Robin radiation boundary; the outer boundary is reflecting or absorbing. Three first-passage problems are solved analytically by quadrature: the mean reaction time, the reaction-before-escape probability, and the conditional success time, the last encoded by a Doob transform that exposes the selection bias of conditioning on capture. The theory separates thermodynamic inputs from conditional parameters and reveals a reaction-limited to diffusion-limited crossover controlled by the local Damk\"ohler number. For typical virus and nanoparticle parameters, the depletion well reaches $2$-$6\,k_{\rm B}T$, capture times are $0.1$-$1\,{\rm ms}$, and the conditional success time is measurably shorter than the unconditional mean. Finite-volume and Chebyshev schemes reproduce the analytic results within their discretization errors and satisfy the radiation-boundary mass balance. This provides a quantitative theoretical framework for crowding-assisted capture prior to membrane wrapping and a reference for comparing crowding, near-wall mobility, and surface reactivity in endocytosis.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu

item.title: An Electrolyte Equation of State Based on openCOSMO-RS: From Aqueous Solutions to Non-Aqueous Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.01686v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predictive COSMO-RS-based electrolyte models such as COSMO-RS-ES describe electrolyte solutions from quantum-chemical information, but treat the liquid as incompressible and give no access to densities or pressure effects. This work presents openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi, to our knowledge the first open-source implementation of a predictive electrolyte equation of state based on openCOSMO-RS. It combines the COSMO-RS-based equation of state openCOSMO-RS-Phi with the ion interaction energies and the long-range term of COSMO-RS-ES, which is first refitted on the same simplified short range. With this refit, a dielectric decrement improves the mean ionic activity coefficients (MIAC), whereas a Born term counts the solvation of the ions a second time and is therefore left out. The equation of state then adds only volume, dispersion and temperature parameters of the ions, fitted to aqueous MIAC and densities. openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi reproduces COSMO-RS-ES in dilute aqueous solutions, improves on it in concentrated ones and also yields solution densities. Extrapolating from aqueous systems, it predicts the MIAC in water + cosolvent mixtures as accurately as the fitted COSMO-RS-ES, as well as the MIAC and bubble points of a benchmark database of water-alcohol-salt systems. Salting-out of organic components is not described as accurately, and salts come out too soluble in organic solvents. Overall, the interaction model developed for COSMO-RS-ES carries over to a large extent to an equation of state, which makes openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi a sound base model for further development, with ion transfer between solvents as a clear target for fitting to non-aqueous data.
item.dc:creator: Leander Rausdzus, Simon M\"uller

item.title: FLAKE: Friction and Lattice Analysis of Kinetics and Energetics of rigid 2D clusters on crystalline substrates
item.description: arXiv:2611.01805v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When a small solid island slides across a crystalline surface, the outcome (smooth flow or stick-slip, free rotation or angular locking) is controlled almost entirely by the geometric relationship between the island and the surface: their relative orientation, size and lattice symmetry. These phenomena are central to nanoscale friction, to the interpretation of colloidal monolayer experiments and to structural superlubricity. FLAKE (Friction and Lattice Analysis of Kinetics and Energetics) is a Python package for simulating the statics and Langevin dynamics of a rigid 2D cluster sliding over a periodic or quasiperiodic substrate potential. It enables fast, systematic exploration of how geometry and substrate symmetry control the energy landscape and friction, studies that are prohibitively expensive with fully atomistic simulations. FLAKE has been the primary simulation tool for three published studies on structural superlubricity and colloidal friction.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Silva

item.title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures
item.description: arXiv:2611.02115v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a computational framework to investigate the flow kinematics of viscoplastic materials, described by the Herschel-Bulkley model, in vane-in-cup rheometers. Numerical simulations are performed using augmented Lagrangian finite element and regularised finite volume methods for two- and three-dimensional configurations, respectively, to characterise the hydrodynamics and yielding behaviour over a broad range of effective parameters. Three types of vanes are investigated: conventional 4- and 6-arm bespoke vanes and a 24-arm fractal vane (Owens et al., J. Rheol., vol. 64(3), 2020, 643-662). Our previous two-dimensional study (Chaparian et al., J. Non-Newtonian Fluid Mech., vol. 307, 2022, 104857) demonstrated the superiority of the fractal vane over conventional N-arm designs. The bespoke vanes produce highly non-uniform yielding, leading to significant deviations from the circular Couette analogy, whereas the 24-arm fractal vane generates nearly axisymmetric yield surfaces that effectively "cloak" the vane geometry. Consequently, the resulting flow closely resembles the azimuthal shear in a conventional "bob & cup" rheometer, providing substantially more accurate rheological measurements. Building on these findings, the present study revisits the torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain rate conversions used in vane-in-cup rheometry. In particular, we re-examine the circular Couette analogy that underpins both the physical interpretation of the flow and the extraction of flow curves from raw rheometric data. Based on our extensive two- and three-dimensional simulations, we identify limitations of the existing conversion relations and propose improved closure expressions that enable more accurate determination of material's rheological properties. Furthermore, the three-dimensional flow structures and yielding patterns within the vane-in-cup fixtures are characterised.
item.dc:creator: James Malcolm, Clare McColgan, Emma Mullarkey, Emad Chaparian

item.title: Noise-resilient collective order through temporal memory in self-propelled particles
item.description: arXiv:2611.03003v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Temporal memory can stabilise collective motion by filtering noisy local observations, but persistent information can also impede adaptation when the collective state changes. We investigate this competition in Vicsek-type systems using two distinct alignment rules: a finite buffer of past observations and a recursive update of an internal directional state. In both models, increasing effective memory shifts the loss of polar order to stronger noise and can restore ordered motion under conditions for which the corresponding memoryless Vicsek model is disordered. The stationary responses of the two models show an approximate correspondence when parameterised by a kernel-based effective memory, consistent with temporal averaging playing a common role in their ordering behaviour rather than from the details of the memory implementation. Their transient dynamics, however, are not determined by effective memory alone. Following a collective perturbation, recovery is fastest at an intermediate memory depth and becomes slower when outdated observations are retained too strongly. Temporal integration therefore produces a trade-off: deeper memory improves noise resilience, whereas excessive persistence reduces responsiveness. These results identify memory depth as a control parameter that separates the optimisation of stationary order from that of dynamical recovery in noisy active systems.
item.dc:creator: Mihir Durve, Sauro Succi, Antonio Celani

item.title: Density and Current Fluctuations for Run-and-Tumble Particles With and Without Interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.03187v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study density and current fluctuations in a one-dimensional gas of run-and-tumble particles (RTPs), whose intrinsic velocities switch between two opposite values at a constant rate. We consider particles with and without pair interactions, including regularized Riesz gases, and also obtain corresponding results for Brownian particles. By linearizing the Dean-Kawasaki (DK) equations around a homogeneous stationary state, we compute density correlations and the variance of the integrated current through the origin. For repulsive Riesz interactions decaying as $1/|x|^s$ with $s>0$, this variance grows at long times as $t^{1/2}$ for $s>1$, but as $t^{s/(1+s)}$ for $0<s<1$. Starting from the same DK description, but retaining the Poisson statistics of direction reversals, we derive a macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT) for RTPs with smooth pair interaction potential, which allows to compute the large time large deviation of the time integrated current. We show that, in the absence of interactions, the MFT saddle point equations can be solved explicitly using a generalized Cole-Hopf transform. This allows to recover and generalize previous results for the current distribution obtained by microscopic calculations, for RTPs with annealed or quenched step initial conditions. Beyond these distributions, MFT allows to compute the optimal density histories producing a prescribed current through the origin. We find that these density profiles, for both RTPs and Brownian particles, exhibit a nontrivial space-time structure. We also study stationary current fluctuations on an interval connected to reservoirs. Finally, we analyze the MFT equations perturbatively in the interaction. In both the infinite-line and reservoir geometries, we obtain explicit first-order corrections to the current generating functions for short-range interacting RTPs and Brownian particles.
item.dc:creator: L\'eo Touzo, Gregory Schehr, Pierre Le Doussal

item.title: Mechano-chemical control of enzymatic activity in crowded environments
item.description: arXiv:2611.03239v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Macromolecular crowding has long been known to alter biochemical equilibria and enzyme kinetics, with reported catalytic activities that may increase, decrease, or vary non-monotonically with crowder concentration. Classical Michaelis--Menten kinetics does not by itself identify which of these responses should occur for a conformationally active enzyme. Here, we develop a minimal non-equilibrium mechano-chemical theory for a fueled enzyme embedded in a bath of passive crowders and uncover a fluctuation-induced effective force dipole acting on the enzyme subunits, akin to a generalized form of dispersion or depletion interaction. Since the preferred conformation of the model enzyme varies through the catalytic cycle, the fluctuation-induced mechanical load affects the relevant kinetic activation barriers and is sufficient to produce both monotonic inhibition and non-monotonic modification of turnover. The framework provides a thermodynamically consistent route for linking crowded environments to catalytic currents, suggesting how mechanical design principles could be leveraged to control enzymatic pathways.
item.dc:creator: Michalis Chatzittofi, Luca Cocconi, Jakob Metson, Ramin Golestanian

item.title: Dynamics of a two-dimensional microswimmer near a slippery boundary
item.description: arXiv:2611.03243v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Microswimmers near walls and interfaces can switch between qualitatively different modes of motion depending on the slip properties of the neighbouring boundaries. To study this theoretically, a two-dimensional point-singularity model of a microswimmer, which does not self-propel in unbounded fluid, is placed near a flat viscosity discontinuity between two fluids with viscosity ratio $\sigma$, and also near a partial-slip wall with Navier-slip length $\lambda$. Using complex-variable methods, the dynamical systems governing the swimmer motion are derived explicitly in both scenarios. Near the viscosity discontinuity, below a universal critical viscosity ratio $\sigma_c=1/2$, the swimmer is trapped at a fixed height with its stresslet axis normal to the boundary. When $\sigma=\sigma_c$ it glides parallel to the boundary at a speed selected by its orientation, with a terminal speed determined by its initial state. For $\sigma>\sigma_c$ it oscillates periodically in height and orientation while drifting along the boundary. The dynamics near a partial-slip wall depend on the ratio of the slip length to the length scale of the singularity and are similar in exhibiting an analogous transition at a critical slip length. It is found, however, that the dynamics near a viscosity discontinuity for $\sigma$ above $\sigma_c$ are richer than those near the partial-slip boundary, including the existence of a hydrodynamic bound state with zero net displacement over one period. Although the study is limited to two dimensions, these results show how a single boundary parameter organises qualitatively distinct modes of locomotion, in close analogy with slip-induced transitions reported for three-dimensional swimmers.
item.dc:creator: Takahiro Kanazawa, Darren Crowdy

item.title: Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)
item.description: arXiv:2611.03542v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. That way, vfNN bypasses solving the equations of motion (a.k.a. the Euler-Lagrange equations), which are in the form of differential equations. To this end, our approach is fundamentally different from conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINN) that solve differential equations by minimizing a phenomenological loss function involving higher order derivatives and ad hoc weight factors. In contrast, vfNN merely evaluates lower order derivatives of the generating functional and replaces the weight factors with rigorous physical scales. This also fundamentally changes the loss landscape, and the desired solutions may become unstable. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. Our simulations using vfNN give accurate results for benchmark systems governed by linear or nonlinear ordinary differential equations.
item.dc:creator: Chinmay Katke, C. Nadir Kaplan

item.title: Emergent Elasticity and Quasiconformal Flow in Active Solids
item.description: arXiv:2601.08968v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Elasticity theory rests on a constitutive relation between stress and strain relative to a reference state. Living matter, however, generates forces by motor molecule activity independent of strain, requiring a different approach to active tissue mechanics. We develop a theory of two-dimensional continuum mechanics in which the active force configuration, not a reference shape, is the fundamental input. Motivated by the cell-level Active Tension Network model for epithelia, we encode motor-driven intercellular forces in a Riemannian tension metric, whose mapping into physical space relates macroscopic stress to the microscopic tensions. Assuming force balance, we show that a stress-free reference state and an effective stress-strain relation emerge at the tissue scale, making the system an effectively elastic active solid. Extending from statics to dynamics, we show how such a solid can morph its shape through adiabatic evolution of active tensions. To capture plastic cell rearrangement, we introduce a second metric representing the cell adjacency graph in the continuum; topological rearrangement then appears as a continuous reparametrization of the tension manifold. The key fields characterizing the tissue's local mechanical state - tension anisotropy, macroscopic stress, and cell shape - arise from the discrepancies between the tension, adjacency, and physical metrics, represented mathematically by quasiconformal maps. Our theory explains how local contractility controls tissue shape and yields predictions distinct from existing models: tissues can remain rigid while "flowing", with a speed set by the rate of change of active forces rather than their magnitude, and shear flow can occur even under isotropic stress, since macroscopic stress is distinct from local tension anisotropy.
item.dc:creator: Nikolas H. Claussen, Fridtjof Brauns, Boris I. Shraiman

item.title: A Vibrated Compacting Granular System: A DEM Light Scattering Comparison
item.description: arXiv:2603.01921v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We perform Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations of granular particles (polystyrene spheres) vibrated inside a cubic container. The study investigates the evolution of the packing fraction with and without rotational friction at different shaking amplitudes. The mean-squared displacement (MSD) is used to analyze the particles' diffusive, subdiffusive, and superdiffusive behavior. By monitoring both the dynamics and density evolution, one can observe the system's glassification. The comparison with experiments shows that the MSDs from the simulations are significantly higher than the MSDs measured by Diffusing Wave Spectroscopy (DWS) \cite{kunzner2025dynamics}. Following our finding that the rotational MSD is of the same order of magnitude as the MSD measured in DWS experiments, we propose that the experimental signal is not dominated by translational motion but rather by rotational particle dynamics. This provides access to a relevant particle property that has previously been difficult to measure directly. Finally, we conclude that the system reaches a dynamically constrained state well before random close packing, with particle displacements already below the Lindemann length.
item.dc:creator: Linnea Heitmeier, Jan Philipp Gabriel

item.title: Particle-scale structure of granular suspensions
item.description: arXiv:2607.18090v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Granular suspensions are intrinsically nonequilibrium systems in which dissipative grain-grain collisions coexist with solvent-induced forcing. We study the particle-scale structure of a granular suspension modeled by smooth inelastic hard spheres immersed in a thermal bath and compare Langevin-dynamics simulation results for the radial distribution function $g(r)$ and the static structure factor $S(q)$ with predictions of an equilibrium-inspired rational function approximation (RFA). The equilibrium hard-sphere RFA is supplied with nonequilibrium input for the contact value and a reduced isothermal-compressibility-like quantity, yielding analytical expressions for $g(r)$ in Laplace space and for $S(q)$. We find that the RFA gives a very good description of the short- and intermediate-range structure of the suspension over a broad range of densities, drag coefficients, and inelasticities. It reproduces $g(r)$ substantially better than the Percus-Yevick approximation in inelastic states, especially near contact, and gives a good account of $S(q)$ except at the smallest wave numbers. There, simulations show a drag-dependent enhancement over the RFA prediction, indicating additional long-wavelength nonequilibrium correlations beyond the present equilibrium-like description. These results show that an equilibrium-based hard-sphere approach provides an accurate description of the particle-scale structure of the present Langevin model with inelastic hard spheres (except in the smallest-$q$ region), and suggest that similar equilibrium-inspired approaches may also be useful for related nonequilibrium hard-sphere suspension models, including multicomponent systems.
item.dc:creator: Santos Bravo Yuste, Antonio M. Puertas

item.title: Benchmarking the flow of epithelial cell monolayer with self-aligning deformable active membranes
item.description: arXiv:2608.13720v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Collective cell migration emerges from the interplay between motility, deformability and mechanical interactions, yet incorporating these ingredients into computationally efficient tissue models remains challenging. Here, we benchmark self-aligning deformable active membranes in a confined-flow geometry that mimics epithelial monolayer migration around a circular obstacle. In this model, cells are represented as deformable, adhesive membranes whose self-propulsion direction relaxes towards their velocity. By systematically varying the self-alignment timescale, cell-cell adhesion and inlet forcing, we characterize the resulting flows through collective alignment, relative density, neighbor rearrangements and spatial velocity fields. The model captures a broad spectrum of tissue behaviors, ranging from disordered, liquid-like flows to highly aligned, solid-like states. Compared with a related multiparticle model, self-aligning active membranes achieve stronger collective alignment, exhibit a more systematic density response and access states closer to both limits of the solid-liquid spectrum. We further show that increasing the target shape index promotes cell elongation and accelerates tissue flow, directly linking cell-scale deformability to tissue-scale transport. Finally, we compare simulated velocity profiles with experimental measurements from in vitro migrating MDCK epithelial cell monolayers and find qualitative agreement across multiple horizontal and vertical transects around the obstacle. These results establish self-aligning deformable active membranes as a versatile framework for connecting cell mechanics, shape adaptation and self-alignment to collective tissue migration in confined geometries.
item.dc:creator: Marcos Pasa, Carine P. Beatrici, Fran\c{c}ois Graner, Leonardo G. Brunnet, Emanuel F. Teixeira

item.title: Time-temperature-composition equivalence of the glass transition in digitally mixed 3D-printed polymers
item.description: arXiv:2610.14986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For more than seventy years, time-temperature equivalence (TTE) has enabled a few measurements to describe the linear viscoelasticity of polymers over many decades of frequency. Multimaterial 3D printing now combines elastomeric and glassy resins voxel by voxel into digitally mixed polymers. Composition shifts the glass transition along the frequency axis, as temperature does, but also broadens it and increases the rubbery plateau modulus. A translation, the only operation of TTE, cannot capture these changes. Here we establish a time-temperature-composition equivalence (TTCE) from dynamic mechanical measurements of five compositions of a printed family. A shift of the transition along the reduced-frequency axis, a stretch of its breadth and a normalization between its plateaus collapse the storage modulus onto one master curve. The collapse holds at every measured temperature, frequency and composition, through a single reduced variable. The position and breadth of the transition change linearly with the volume fraction of the glassy resin. The phase angle and the relaxation spectrum superpose with the same parameters, so the family shares one distribution of relaxation times. The resulting closed form gives the storage and loss moduli continuously in composition, temperature and frequency, and quantitatively predicts two further mixtures withheld from the calibration. The same shift, stretch and normalization also collapse published temperature sweeps of a patterned composite family of different resins, pointing to broader applicability. Composition thus joins temperature and frequency as a third variable of one equivalence, and the closed form can guide the design of graded and architected printed structures.
item.dc:creator: Beijun Shen, Sanat K. Kumar, Mary C. Boyce

item.title: Bounded entropy production constrains hierarchical decision-making in homing pigeon flocks
item.description: arXiv:2610.31126v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Collective decision-making requires individuals to reconcile diverse, often conflicting opinions to reach a common course of action. However, within a group, individuals rarely exert equal influence, leading to non-reciprocal communication patterns manifested as leader-follower relationships and social hierarchies. Here, using homing pigeon flocks as a model system, we develop a trajectory-based framework to infer and quantify hierarchy within navigating living collectives. We find that while small flocks exhibit pronounced hierarchy, increasing flock size progressively weakens it, driving the collective toward more egalitarian decision-making. We provide a physical rationale for this observation using a thermodynamic framework in which non-reciprocal communication between birds carries an information-entropy cost. Our calculations reveal that hierarchy weakening observed in larger flocks is consistent with maintaining a constant per-individual entropy production rate across flock sizes. Together, these results suggest that constraints on information-processing capacity may play an important role in the collective dynamics of living organisms.
item.dc:creator: Bibaswan Ghosh, Vipul Rai, Harsh Soni, Nitin Kumar

item.title: Odd-viscosity-induced instability in shear flows
item.description: arXiv:2609.01566v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Odd viscosity is a nondissipative component of the viscosity tensor that arises in fluids with broken time-reversal symmetry. We show that, despite being energy-conserving, odd viscosity can qualitatively alter hydrodynamic stability by generating exponentially growing modes that are absent in conventional fluids. For plane Poiseuille flow, we derive the odd-viscous generalization of the Orr--Sommerfeld--Squire equations and find a new instability that first emerges for streamwise-uniform modes and extends to oblique modes. The instability exploits the non-normality of the linearized Navier--Stokes operator: conventional fluids support transiently growing disturbances through the lift-up mechanism, while odd viscosity closes a feedback loop between wall-normal velocity and vorticity, converting these disturbances into self-sustaining exponentially growing modes. This mechanism lowers the linear instability threshold by nearly two orders of magnitude, from $\mathrm{Re}_c \approx 5772$ to $\mathrm{Re}_c \approx 62$. More generally, we show that an energy-conserving coupling can destabilize a linearly stable system by sustaining the growth of otherwise transiently growing disturbances. Such a coupling thus triggers energy growth without directly supplying energy, by enabling continuous energy extraction from the background state. This establishes a mechanism for controlling stability in non-normal systems without direct energy dissipation or injection.
item.dc:creator: Yonatan Messica, Igor Gornyi, Dmitri B. Gutman

item.title: Quantifying translational and bond-orientational order metrics in hyperuniform and nonhyperuniform many-particle systems
item.description: arXiv:2609.10359v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantifying the degree of order/disorder in many-particle systems remains an outstanding problem in physics, materials science, and mathematics. To this end, we consider the translational order metric $\tau_T$, defined as the squared $L^2$ norm of the total correlation function $h(\mathbf{r})$, and introduce its bond-orientational analogue $\tau_O$, defined from the weighted total correlation function $h_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{r})$ using local orientational weights (S. Torquato et al., Phys. Rev. X 16, 011042 (2026)). The pair $(\tau_T,\tau_O)$ places both forms of order on a common two-point statistical footing. We compute both metrics for two nonhyperuniform sphere-packing models in 2D and 3D as functions of packing fraction $\phi$: 1) equilibrium hard particles and 2) nonequilibrium random sequential addition (RSA) packings. For the nonhyperuniform systems, bond-orientational order remains subdominant along the equilibrium-fluid and RSA configurations; however, its magnitude relative to the translational metric increases near the upper end of the equilibrium-fluid branches, much more strongly in 2D than in 3D, and the two metrics become comparable along the sampled crystal branches. At common packing fractions, equilibrium fluids and RSA packings trace distinct $(\tau_T,\tau_O)$ trajectories, revealing preparation-dependent differences in structural order. As a representative hyperuniform family, we study 2D disordered stealthy hyperuniform (SHU) ground states for $0<\chi<1/2$, where $\chi$ is the stealthiness parameter. Within the disordered SHU phase, bond-orientational order remains subdominant, but its magnitude relative to the translational metric increases toward the disorder-to-order threshold. In all three models, $\tau_T$ and $\tau_O$ are positively correlated beyond the Poisson-reference regime: $\tau_O$ increases monotonically with $\tau_T$ across the sampled state points.
item.dc:creator: Anirban Mukherjee, Salvatore Torquato

item.title: Ideal interaction dynamics of defects and background fields in condensed matter
item.description: arXiv:2610.32973v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While defect dynamics in condensed matter systems is widely studied and several methods are available to track the defect position over time, the formulation of dynamical models for the coupled evolution of both defects and background field quantities seems to be more challenging. Yet, the overall behavior of a system containing moving defects is strongly influenced by this defect-field interaction. Here, we propose a modeling framework for the conservative coupled evolution of the defect density and the background fields upon focusing on two relevant cases of study: the Gross-Pitaevskii theory of quantum fluids and the Ericksen-Leslie model of nematic liquid crystals. To achieve the coupled evolution, we combine the Euler-Poincar\'e variational setting of continuum dynamics with the gauge theory of topological defects. While the latter allows us to overcome certain ambiguities in definition of the defect density, the Euler-Poincar\'e method provides a unified modeling approach in the absence of defect reconnection. Suitable variational regularizations are also proposed to deal with the motion of singular defect lines.
item.dc:creator: Fran\c{c}ois Gay-Balmaz, Tudor S. Ratiu, Cesare Tronci
